label: Spherical and Euclidean Buildings
notes: This appendix to II.10 spans printed pages 342 through 346 and introduces buildings as highly symmetric simplicial complexes. The headline is that local chamber combinatorics governs global curvature: spherical buildings are CAT(1) and Euclidean buildings are CAT(0). We motivate the whole apparatus through apartments glued along chambers.

label: Coxeter Complexes
notes: Before buildings we need apartments, and an apartment is a Coxeter complex. A finite reflection group tiles a sphere; an affine reflection group tiles Euclidean space. Stress that the walls are the reflection hyperplanes and the chambers are the connected pieces of their complement, all permuted simply transitively by the group.

label: Chambers, Walls, Galleries
notes: Here we fix the combinatorial vocabulary that runs through the appendix. Chambers are top-dimensional simplices, panels are their codimension-one faces, walls separate chambers, and a gallery is a chamber-to-chamber path crossing one wall at a time. Gallery distance counts crossings and will measure metric distance later.

label: The Building Axioms
notes: Now the definition. A building is a simplicial complex with a system of apartments, each isomorphic to a fixed Coxeter complex, such that any two simplices lie in a common apartment and any two apartments are isomorphic fixing their intersection. Emphasise that these two axioms force the strong homogeneity buildings are famous for.

label: Retractions onto Apartments
notes: Retractions are the technical engine. Fixing an apartment and a chamber, one folds the whole building onto that apartment, preserving gallery distance from the base chamber. Explain that retractions let us transport metric and combinatorial computations from the complicated building into a single well-understood Coxeter complex.

label: Spherical Buildings are CAT(1)
notes: For a spherical building the Coxeter complex is a sphere tiled by a finite reflection group, so each apartment carries the round metric of curvature one. The gluing of apartments along chambers is an isometric gluing, and the appendix records that the resulting complex is CAT(1), the spherical-curvature comparison space.

label: Euclidean Buildings are CAT(0)
notes: Euclidean or affine buildings replace the sphere by Euclidean space tiled by an affine reflection group, the A2 triangular tiling being the prototype. Each apartment is flat, the gluing is isometric, and the building is CAT(0): complete, contractible, with unique geodesics. This is the non-positive-curvature payoff of the appendix.

label: Links and the Curvature Test
notes: Walk through why the curvature bound holds. By the link condition a Euclidean building is CAT(0) exactly when every vertex link is CAT(1), and those links are themselves spherical buildings. So the two halves of the appendix interlock: spherical buildings certify the curvature of Euclidean buildings one dimension up.

label: Buildings of Algebraic Groups
notes: The motivating examples come from algebra. SL(n) over a field gives a spherical building from the flags of subspaces; over a local field SL(n) gives a Euclidean building from lattice classes. Stress that the Weyl group of the algebraic group is exactly the Coxeter group tiling each apartment, tying combinatorics to representation theory.

label: Tits Boundary and Rank
notes: Spherical buildings reappear at infinity. The Tits boundary of a higher-rank symmetric space or of a Euclidean building is a spherical building, encoding asymptotic directions. Rigidity theorems read symmetry of the boundary building back into the interior, which is why buildings sit at the center of higher-rank geometry.

label: Recap and the Computational Model
notes: Recap the dictionary: apartment equals Coxeter complex, chamber equals top cell, gallery distance equals combinatorial metric, spherical equals CAT(1), Euclidean equals CAT(0). The notebook builds a small chamber graph and computes gallery distances, turning each definition into an inspectable invariant rather than a slogan.
